Alright, the end‑to‑end training probe (test_full_pipeline_end_to_end) is still not completing. The previous attempts to run it directly via the pipeline script resulted in a hung process (PID 2694471) that consumed ~19 GB of GPU memory and ultimately dumped core when I tried to extract more detailed traces. My attempts to grep for relevant frames only returned pytest/pluggy noise, and the raw output contains a massive list of loaded extension modules followed by a timeout dump, which tells me the test never got far enough to produce any of the application‑level logs (e.g., “train”, “forward”, “benchmark”, etc.) that I need to diagnose the stall.

Given that the test seems to get stuck early—perhaps in the lazy initialization of the sparse‑attention or FP4 quantization components—I need a more controlled way to run it that:

1. Limits the total runtime so it won’t consume resources indefinitely.
2. Captures stdout/stderr unbuffered so I can see incremental progress.
3. Allows me to peek at the log after a reasonable warm‑up period (say 45 seconds) to confirm that the test is making headway or to catch the point where it hangs.

The `timeout` utility is perfect for bounding the overall run; a 10‑minute limit (`timeout 600`) should be generous enough for the full pipeline under normal conditions, yet short enough to avoid runaway GPU usage. I’ll invoke the test module directly with `pytest -q -s` (quiet, but still show prints) and pipe all output to a temporary log file (`/tmp/pipe_probe.log`). Running it in the background (`&`) lets me continue issuing commands without blocking.

Immediately after launching, I’ll print a simple “started” marker so I know the background job has been scheduled, then pause (`sleep 45`) to give the test time to initialize and start processing. After the pause, I’ll read the log, convert any carriage returns to newlines (the test sometimes uses `\r` for progress bars), filter out noisy lines (those containing `%` or the typical pytest/pluggy boilerplate), and display the last ten lines. This should give me a concise snapshot of whatever the test is doing at that moment—whether it’s loading the model, beginning training, or still stuck in some initialization loop.

I also need to set a generous timeout for the overall tool call itself (70 000 ms) because the background process will continue running while I’m sleeping and tailing the log; the tool call must stay alive long enough to complete the `sleep 45` and the final `tail`. Using `timeout: 70000` (70 seconds) comfortably exceeds the 45‑second sleep plus a buffer for the log processing.

All of this together should give me a clear, timely view of the pipeline’s behavior without risking another indefinite hang.

Therefore, I’ll issue the following Bash command: run the test with `timeout 600`, redirect output, background it, echo “started”, sleep 45 seconds, then process the log and show the tail.ASSISTANT (tool call) Bash input={"command": "timeout 600 .venv/bin/python -u -m pytest tests/e2e/test_train_entry.py::test_full_pipeline_end_to_end -q -s > /tmp/pipe_probe.log 2>&1 &\necho started; sleep 45; tr '\\r' '\\n' < /tmp/pipe_probe.log | grep -v \"%|\" | grep . | tail -10", "description": "Unbuffered pipeline probe, peek after 45s", "timeout": 70000}
